subject: Animation
title: Phil Tippett: From Stop-Motion to Digital
description: A short lesson to help you apply Phil Tippett: From Stop-Motion to Digital.

hook.text: Phil Tippett animated the AT-AT walkers in The Empire Strikes Back using go-motion, an upgraded stop-motion.

buildup.text: Go-motion added motion blur by slightly moving puppets during exposure, creating smoother movement.

discovery.text: Tippett was hired for Jurassic Park to animate dinosaurs with go-motion techniques.

twist.text: When he saw the CGI tests, Tippett famously told Spielberg: I think I'm extinct.

climax.text: Spielberg kept Tippett on to supervise the CGI dinosaurs, bridging analog artistry and digital tools.

punchline.text: The man who thought he was extinct helped birth a new era.

quiz.question: What did Phil Tippett famously say when he saw the CGI dinosaur tests for Jurassic Park?
options: This is the future of filmmaking

details.summary: Phil Tippett was a master stop-motion animator who transitioned to digital effects. He animated the AT-AT walkers in The Empire Strikes Back and later pioneered the dinosaur input device for Jurassic Park's CGI creatures.
details.whyItMatters: Tippett's career bridges analog and digital eras. His stop-motion sensibility informed digital creature animation, proving that the artistry behind stop-motion transcends any particular technology.
takeaways: Tippett animated iconic Star Wars creatures using stop-motion
He transitioned to digital by creating go-motion and DID systems
His stop-motion expertise improved the quality of early CGI creatures

faq.question: What is the dinosaur input device that Tippett created?
faq.answer: It was a physical armature connected to a computer. Tippett could pose the puppet by hand, and the computer recorded the movements as digital animation data. It let stop-motion artists work naturally while creating CGI output.

faq.question: What is go-motion and how does it differ from stop-motion?
faq.answer: Tippett invented go-motion to add motion blur to stop-motion puppets. A computer moved the puppet slightly during each frame exposure, creating natural blur instead of the crisp, slightly jerky look of traditional stop-motion.
